newsitem.title: USA: Columbia/HCA earnings rise despite troubles.
newsitem.headline: Columbia/HCA earnings rise despite troubles.

text.p: Columbia/HCA Healthcare Corp., under investigation for fraud, said Wednesday that earnings rose 13 percent in the second quarter and that it was dropping plans to buy a majority stake in a health news cable channel.

The announcements came just days after Chief Executive Officer Richard Scott and President David Vandewater resigned under pressure amid probes into possible Medicare fraud by the company, the nation's largest for-profit hospital chain.
The company, based in Nashville, on Friday named its vice chairman, Dr. Thomas Frist, 58, as chairman and CEO.
Despite the troubles, the company's earnings matched expectations on Wall Street and some of its financial results continued to outperform other for-profit hospital chains.

Columbia said net income rose to $412 million, or 62 cents a share, in the quarter, from $364 million, or 54 cents a share, a year earlier. The results matched forecasts of 62 cents a share, according to First Call, which tracks analysts' estimates.
Sales grew to $5.2 billion from $4.9 billion, the company said. Revenues at hospitals open at least a year rose 6 percent, the company said.
Columbia historically has enjoyed same-hospital revenue growth of 7 percent to 11 percent vs. the industry average of about 5 percent.

Columbia also said it had decided not to proceed with an agreement announced May 13 to buy a majority interest in America's Health Network, a 24-hour health news cable channel, from A.H. Belo Corp., based in Dallas. Terms were not disclosed.

Various federal agencies are looking into Columbia's laboratory billing, home health care and Medicare-related business practices for possible fraud. The attorneys general of Texas and Alabama are conducting their own investigations.
Scott and Vandewater resigned under fire from board members dissatisfied with the company's handling of the investigation and other matters.
Columbia also said that as of June 30 it had spent $730 million repurchasing its stock as part of a $1 billion repurchase programme started in April.
Columbia stock fell 62.5 cents to $33.875 in midday consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
